Published - August 16, 2026 10:18 pm IST - Bucharest AFP READ LATER SEE ALL Remove A Spanish fighter jet on Sunday (August 16, 2026) shot down a drone that had breached Romanian airspace near the border with Ukraine and Moldova, national authorities and NATO said. A growing number of drones have crossed into NATO states in eastern Europe as Russia pursues its invasion of Ukraine. The interception of the drone — which entered from Moldova — was carried out by an F-18, deployed on NATO duties, at 5:01 am (0201 GMT), the Romanian defence ministry said in a statement. Debris fell in an unpopulated area of the Galati region, near the Ukrainian border, it added. Spain's Defence Ministry said on X that its air force had shown "its outstanding professionalism in the defence of European airspace". Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said he had spoken with his Romanian counterpart Oana Toiu, who thanked the pilots. NATO Air Command said on X that the mission involved two F-18s, which are part of a Spanish contingent of around 200 personnel and 11 aircraft based in Romania. Romania's eastern seaboard, bordering the Black Sea, is close to areas frequently targeted by Russian strikes. This was the fourth drone to be destroyed in the country since the start of Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022. And, in a separate incident on Sunday (August 16, 2026) announced by the defence ministry, drone debris was found in the Black Sea, off Romania's city of Constanta. In July, Romania expelled a Russian embassy employee in what it called "a firm response" to drones repeatedly breaching the country's airspace. Romania shot down three drones on three consecutive days before the expulsion. Authorities have reported finding drone fragments on Romanian soil several times since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube River, which lie just across the border. Similar incidents have been reported elsewhere on NATO's eastern flank, including in Poland and the Baltic states. On Friday (August 14, 2026), NATO said Italian jets operating under the alliance's air-policing mission shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA View image in fullscreen Members of the community gather at Heaton Park Hebrew Synagogue in Crumpsall, Manchester, a week after the terror attack in October last year. Photograph: Peter Byrne/PA UK news Manchester synagogue attack: ministers seek to block MI5 files from inquest Government lawyers tell coroner disclosing intelligence would pose serious risk to national security Josh Halliday North of England editor Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.07 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ministers are seeking to block intelligence material from being heard at an inquest into the death of two men killed in the 2025 Manchester synagogue attack. Lawyers for Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, told a coroner on Thursday that disclosing the MI5 files would pose a serious risk to national security. Melvin Cravitz, 66, died as a result of multiple knife wounds inflicted by the attacker, Jihad al-Shamie. Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a single police gunshot wound as he held the building’s doors shut against the terrorist. A senior coroner is due to examine the deaths of the two men at the Heaton Park Hebrew synagogue on 2 October last year during Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. The full inquest will focus on al-Shamie’s background, as well as what the state knew about him before the attack. It will also examine security at the synagogue, the role of the state in assessing the risks to the Jewish community in Greater Manchester, and the response to the attack. Mahmood told the Commons on 13 October that al-Shamie was “never referred to the Prevent programme, nor was he known to counter-terrorism policing or the security services”. At a pre-inquest review on Thursday, barristers for the families of Cravitz and Daulby said they were concerned that the emergence of MI5 material “may contradict” that statement. Anna Morris KC, representing Daulby’s family, said there had been a “demonstrable lack of candour” by the security services in other proceedings, including the inquiry into the Manchester Arena attack. She said Daulby’s family were “concerned that this application [by the Home Office] and the information behind it may contradict statements made public by security services and counter-terrorism police that the suspect was not known to counter-terrorism police”. The deaths of Daulby and Cravitz are being examined by Alexia Durran, the chief coroner of England and Wales, at Manchester coroner’s court. Edward Pleeth, counsel to the inquest, told the hearing the government was seeking to withhold “potentially relevant security sensitive material held by MI5” and “potentially relevant security sensitive material held by counter-terrorism police”. Pleeth said this unspecified material was judged by the government to “cause serious harm to national security” if it was disclosed publicly. He said the inquest legal team was satisfied that the information was so sensitive it could not be aired even in a redacted form. There was “no adequate alternative to complete non-disclosure”, Pleeth said, describing the concerns about its disclosure as “well-evidenced”. Durran is now considering whether to ask the government to convert the inquest into a statutory public inquiry to allow the MI5 material to be heard in private. Unlike public inquiries, coroner’s inquests cannot legally consider evidence given in secret hearings. Neil Sheldon KC, representing the Home Office, described the MI5 material as a “discrete body of information” that had been “identified as relevant and has the potential to impact the inquest”. The application to block the information from being heard publicly was not an “extreme approach” but was “cogent, compelling and supported by detailed analysis”, he told the court. Victoria Ailes, representing Cravitz’s family, said his family had “questions in this entire area” and were concerned that this new material came after “statements by the secretary of state to the House of Commons [that al-Shamie] was not known to counter-terrorism police or the security services”. Al-Shamie, a Syrian-born UK citizen, launched the attack while wearing what seemed to be a suicide vest. Before police arrived, the 35-year-old called 999 and pledged allegiance to Islamic State. Last month, a man who conducted hostile reconnaissance at a military base alongside al-Shamie was jailed for life with a minimum term of 16 years, after admitting preparing acts of terror. Mohammad Asim Bashir, 31, and al-Shamie travelled by car to the UK Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Swindon, in August last year, two months before the synagogue attack. Bashir was identified when counter-terrorism officers searched al-Shamie’s mobile devices after the Heaton Park attack. However, Greater Manchester police said last month that officers had seized his phones months earlier in 2025 after unrelated arrests, but that they were not examined until after the attack. Another man, Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, was charged on 21 August with failing to disclose information in relation to the synagogue attack. Hakim, 49, pleaded not guilty at Westminster magistrates court. He is due to attend a hearing at the Old Bailey on 25 September. https://prague.tv/prague-now/atms-in-pra.text: Need to know Where Bank branches, shopping centres, stations and stand-alone machines across the city When 24 hours at most machines Getting there Not applicable The short version Always choose to be charged in Czech crowns (CZK), never in your home currency, when a machine or shop terminal offers a choice. Bank-owned machines, ideally at a branch, are safer and usually cheaper than stand-alone machines on tourist streets. Your own bank's foreign fees matter as much as the machine's: check them before you travel. On this page 7 sections What dynamic currency conversion is Which machines are best? Two layers of cost How much cash do you need? ATM or exchange office? Safety at the machine If something goes wrong You insert your card, type your PIN and the screen asks a polite question: would you like to be charged in your home currency or in Czech crowns? One answer looks helpful, because you see your own money and a familiar number. It is also the more expensive answer. This is called dynamic currency conversion, or DCC, and avoiding it is the single most useful habit at a Prague cash machine. What dynamic currency conversion is When you withdraw cash abroad, someone has to convert the crowns you receive into the currency of your account. There are two ways. Your own bank converts the amount after the withdrawal, at its own rate. Or the machine's operator offers to convert it on the spot and shows the result on screen. The second option feels convenient, and that is its trick. The operator sets the rate and often adds a margin, so you pay more than if you had let your bank do the work. The difference does not appear as a separate fee. It is hidden in the rate. The rule is simple. If a machine or card terminal offers a choice, pick Czech crowns (CZK) and decline the conversion. This applies at ATMs, in shops and restaurants, and at hotels. Our paying in Prague guide covers card payments in more detail. Withdrawing money without surprises Find a bank-owned machine Look for machines at or outside a branch of a major Czech bank. They are monitored and generally cheaper. Insert your card and enter your PIN Cover the keypad and check there is nothing odd attached to the card slot. Read the screen before accepting If a fee is shown, decide whether you accept it. If you do not, cancel and try another machine. Choose CZK Decline any offer to convert into your home currency. Take your card and cash Keep the receipt until you have checked your statement. Which machines are best? The safest bet is a machine belonging to a major bank, such as ČSOB, Česká spořitelna or Komerční banka, ideally at a branch. These tend to sit in well-lit places with cameras and proper maintenance. Any fee should be shown on screen before you confirm. Stand-alone machines in tourist areas can charge more. Many are run by independent operators, sit on the busiest streets and exist to make money from visitors. They are not illegal, only expensive. The fee should be shown on screen before you proceed. If it looks high, press cancel and walk to a bank branch, which is rarely far away. Choosing an ATM Type Typical situation What to watch Bank branch machine Outside or inside a bank Usually the best choice Shopping centre machine Inside a mall, usually bank-owned Check who runs it and any fee on screen Stand-alone tourist machine On the busiest streets and squares Higher fees and DCC prompts Airport and station machine Convenient on arrival Check fees and decline conversion General pattern. Always read the screen before confirming. Two layers of cost Withdrawing abroad can involve two sets of charges. The machine may add a fee, which it should show. And your own bank may add a foreign transaction fee, a cash withdrawal fee, or both, plus its own exchange rate. Those are set by your bank, not by Czech law. Before you leave, look at your bank's terms for foreign withdrawals. Some travel-friendly accounts and digital banks offer low or no fees; our digital banking guide compares the approaches. If you are staying a while, opening a Czech account solves the problem; see opening a bank account as a foreigner . For comparison, the Czech National Bank (ČNB) publishes official daily exchange rates. They are a benchmark, not what you will get, but a rate far from it is a warning sign. 'Guaranteed rate' is not a favour A screen that promises 'no fees' or a 'guaranteed rate' in your home currency is usually dynamic currency conversion. Choose CZK and let your own bank convert. How much cash do you need? Probably less than you think. Cards and phone payments work nearly everywhere in Prague, so you may only need cash for small items: a market stall, a tip, a public toilet. Withdraw modest amounts once or twice rather than a large sum, and keep an eye on any fee per withdrawal. Our tipping guide and the guide to public toilets explain where small notes and coins are handy. For the notes themselves, see the Czech koruna for beginners . ATM or exchange office? An ATM at a bank branch often gives you a better deal than a cash exchange. The exchange offices that fill the centre of Prague range from fair to awful, and the worst are very expensive. Our guide to reading an exchange-rate board shows how to tell one from the other, and the main piece on changing money in Prague covers your rights, including the three-hour cancellation right. If you must change cash, do it at a bank, not at a booth near a monument. Safety at the machine Use machines inside bank branches or lobbies when you can. Cover the keypad when you type your PIN. Check the card slot and keypad for anything loose or unusual. If a machine swallows your card, contact your bank immediately and do not accept help from strangers. Watch for people standing too close, and for distraction tactics; our guide to pickpockets and tourist traps guide describe how these work. For a lost or stolen card, call your bank's emergency line. For other emergencies, see emergency numbers and help . If something goes wrong Keep your receipt and take a photo of the machine screen and any sign. Contact your own bank first and explain what happened. If you believe a business misled you about charges, the Czech Trade Inspection Authority (ČOI) handles consumer complaints about shops and services. Complaints about your own bank are for your bank and, if needed, its regulator. Frequently asked questions Should I choose CZK or my home currency at a Prague ATM? Choose CZK. Declining the conversion lets your own bank convert, which is usually cheaper than the machine's offer. Are all ATMs in Prague charging fees? Not necessarily. Fees differ from machine to machine, and your own bank may add its own. Stand-alone machines in tourist areas tend to charge more. The screen should show any fee before you confirm. Is it safe to use an ATM at night? Use machines in well-lit places, ideally in a bank lobby or branch, and cover the keypad. Do I need to carry cash in Prague? A little. Cards work almost everywhere, but small cash helps for tips, markets and public toilets. What if the ATM keeps my card? Contact your bank straight away and block the card if needed. Keep any receipt. https://www.novinite.com/view_news.php?i.text: iNews Novinite Econ DoctorOnline Jenite Div Sporta FitWell Sportuvai Peika Programata News in English BUSINESS POLITICS WORLD SOCIETY SPORTS Latest Culture Crime · Hotels 5* · Hotels 4* · Hotels 3* · Apartment Houses · Bar&Restaurants · Rent-a-car · Casino · Sport · Mountain resorts · Sea resorts · Education · Entertainment · Shopping · Health Clinics · Beauty Zone · Public Safety · Business Finance Best in BG Novinite Insider · Radisson Blu · 4 Seasons · French Survey · Investors Survey · Austrian Survey · Italian Survey · US Survey · Greek Survey · Dutch Survey Special Topics Diplomacy Elections Defense Bulgaria in EU Domestic PM Radev Says Bulgaria Was Ready to Deploy Jets Against the Black Sea Drones Tweet Share Send to Kindle Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Bulgaria was ready to deploy L-39 military aircraft against drones that attacked a commercial vessel in the Black Sea if the unmanned aerial vehicles had entered the country's territorial waters, adding that a French patrol aircraft had detected them at least 30 minutes before the strike. The Bulgarian Air Force had L-39 aircraft stationed in Balchik on standby for a possible response, Radev said as he discussed the recent Black Sea incidents and Bulgaria 's ability to counter such threats. Radev said authorities had obtained video footage of the attack and were examining it in cooperation with allied intelligence services. Forensic analyses are also underway to establish where the drones originated. “We have video footage, which we have shared with our allies. Every possible analysis is currently being conducted. I expect that we will finally have clear evidence as to where these drones came from,” Radev said. The prime minister added that the footage would be released publicly as soon as possible, but stressed that he could not yet identify those responsible for the attack. “We do not yet know where the drone originated. I have shared my logical assumptions with you, but I do not wish to jump to conclusions. I imagine you have seen discussions on social media, where all sorts of theories are circulating - suggesting, for instance, that the drone could belong to any of four or five different countries. However, such claims are not to be taken seriously. We intend to conduct a thorough and credible expert assessment in collaboration with our allies,” Radev said. He described the coordination between the Bulgarian Armed Forces and allied aircraft conducting patrols over the Black Sea , saying a French reconnaissance plane had spotted the drones in time to warn the targeted ship's crew. “We have been in constant communication with NATO, requesting assistance. As you know, there are already aircraft on patrol, including American ones. In fact, the French patrol aircraft spotted the drones at least half an hour before the strike; it detected them and even provided information on their trajectory. This gave the crew of the targeted ship the opportunity to take all necessary evacuation measures,” the prime minister said. Radev said allied forces and the Bulgarian military were exchanging information in real time. He reiterated that Bulgaria had been prepared to respond militarily if the drones had entered its territorial waters. “We were prepared to scramble L-39 aircraft based in Balchik and use their weaponry against these drones , had they entered our territorial waters. But it didn't come to that,” he said. However, Radev warned that Bulgaria 's response options were subject to legal and practical restrictions. International law prevents the country from taking military action outside its own territorial waters, while weather, available equipment, and surveillance capabilities also limit its ability to detect and respond to threats in the exclusive economic zone. “Even if we possess the means to intervene, we cannot, from a strictly legal standpoint, take action outside our own territorial zones. We cannot do so, as it would constitute a violation of international law. Furthermore, there are various limitations regarding the capabilities at our disposal for surveillance, reconnaissance, and the detection of threats within the Exclusive Economic Zone,” Radev said. He also pointed to Bulgaria 's limited naval capacity, which prevents it from maintaining a permanent presence across the entire zone. “Moreover, we are dependent on weather conditions. It is not always possible to fly, nor is it always possible to take action. Our fleet is limited in both number and capabilities. We are unable to maintain a continuous watch across the entire Exclusive Economic Zone,” the prime minister said. Radev seeks additional NATO assistance Radev confirmed that he had discussed the need for further allied support with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. “We are waiting. I have also raised this issue with Mark Rutte. You can see that the quantities of weaponry available to NATO also have their limits. They are stretched from the Baltic Sea, across the land, to the Black Sea. So, everything that can be done is being done,” he said. Bulgaria has also pursued diplomatic action at the highest international level, including through the United Nations, NATO, and European institutions, Radev said. He argued that military measures and allied assistance could reduce risks but would not ensure that attacks on ships stopped. “From this point on, there is only one solution to ensure that these attacks finally come to an end: a ceasefire, sitting down at the negotiating table, and beginning talks. Until that happens, there is no guarantee regarding what can be done,” Radev said. He said the European Union and NATO should support diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending hostilities, citing efforts to open talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, including those by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and the Norwegian prime minister. “The only 100% guarantee is a ceasefire and the political will for dialogue. I believe the European Union and NATO should engage in these efforts,” Radev said. The prime minister also pledged formal diplomatic action if expert assessments establish the drones ' origin and responsibility for the attack. “If the origin of these drones is proven, the Minister of Foreign Affairs will immediately summon the relevant ambassador to deliver a note of protest,” Radev said. Three drones struck a vessel 16 nautical miles off Cape Kaliakra, and its crew was rescued. The incident involved the merchant ship CONTSHIP JET, which was hit on October 28 about 16 nautical miles from the cape. Although the crew survived, the vessel was reported to have sunk the following day. The attack has renewed concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea and the risks to trade routes close to Bulgarian territorial waters. The European Commission also reacted to the attacks on civilian vessels, calling them an “unacceptable escalation” that threatens EU interests, maritime transport, and supply chains. Brussels expressed solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania, warning that the consequences of the war in Ukraine continued to pose serious security risks in the Black Sea region. Radev contrasts Bulgaria 's response with Romania's Radev defended Bulgaria 's decision not to identify a country as responsible for the drone attacks before conclusive evidence was available. He cited Romania, which he said had blamed Russia but subsequently experienced another incident. “ Bulgaria did not make definitive accusations against any country because we lacked concrete evidence at the time. Romania stated that the aggressor and the source of these drones was Russia. Yet, this failed to protect them. The very next day, drones sank a ship—within their own territorial waters, no less. Do you see the difference?” Radev said. He criticized Bulgarian politicians calling for the immediate naming of a suspected perpetrator, arguing that public accusations would not prevent further attacks. “I want to address all our politicians who so convincingly propagate the notion that if we speak out and declare, 'You, Russia, are the source of the attack', if we shake our finger at them, that will protect us. It cannot protect us. Look at what happened in Romania: the very next day, a ship was struck and sunk. And I repeat - this did not happen in the exclusive economic zone, but in territorial waters,” the prime minister said. Radev says government will follow court ruling on CEC complaint Radev also commented on a Central Election Commission (CEC) decision concerning a complaint against him over his support for Iliyana Yotova's candidacy, which had been expressed through the government press office. He said the Council of Ministers would comply with the commission's decision, while noting that the final course of action would depend on the court because the ruling had been appealed. “The Council of Ministers will comply with the decision of the Central Election Commission. Whatever the Bulgarian court decides, that is what we will do,” Radev said.
